questions.question: A small amount of solid lead iodide was added to water and stirred. Most settled but a little dissolved, establishing $\text{PbI}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{I}^-(aq)$. The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are shown. What happened at time $t$?
questions.answer: Adding water dilutes the ions, so the reverse (precipitation) rate drops and then recovers; the dissolution rate is unchanged.
options: A small amount of water was added.

questions.question: What is the pH of a 0.010 mol L⁻¹ solution of a weak monoprotic acid that is 4.0% ionised?
20.00 mL samples of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $\text{HNO}_3$ (both strong) and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (weak) were separately titrated with 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. To react completely:
questions.answer: The amount depends on moles of ionisable H: sulfuric acid is diprotic; acid strength does not matter.
options: all three acids require the same amount of NaOH.
$\text{HNO}_3$ requires more than $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ but less than $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ require the same amount but $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ less.
$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ require the same amount but $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ more.

questions.question: $\text{CO}(g)+2\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$ is exothermic. An equilibrium mixture at 400 °C in a closed container is changed to 450 °C. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Higher temperature raises the pressure and shifts equilibrium left, producing more gas molecules.
options: The total number of molecules decreases.
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions remain constant.
The pressure of the gaseous mixture increases.
The rate of formation of hydrogen decreases while the rate of decomposition of methanol increases.

questions.question: Which compound gives the ¹³C NMR spectrum shown?
questions.answer: Three signals, all in the alkyl region (about 14–32 ppm): hexane has three carbon environments.

questions.question: A student prepares a standard solution: (i) 2.5 g of NaOH is dissolved in water in a beaker; (ii) the solution is funnelled into a volumetric flask and the beaker and funnel set aside without washing; (iii) the flask is filled with water to slightly over the calibration line; (iv) the flask is shaken. Compared with the calculated value, the solution is likely to be:
questions.answer: Some NaOH is left behind and the volume is too large, so the concentration is lower. (Strength is not the same as concentration.)

questions.question:
Arrange these reactions in order of **increasing** tendency to reach completion.

I: $4\text{NH}_3+3\text{O}_2\rightleftharpoons2\text{N}_2+6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $K=1.0\times10^{228}$
II: $2\text{HF}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_2+\text{F}_2$, $K=1.0\times10^{-13}$
III: $2\text{NOCl}\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}+\text{Cl}_2$, $K=4.7\times10^{-4}$
IV: $\text{N}_2+\text{O}_2\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}$, $K=5.0\times10^{-31}$
questions.answer: A larger $K$ means a greater extent of reaction: IV < II < III < I.

questions.question: Acidified potassium permanganate oxidises an alkene. What colour change is observed?
questions.answer: Purple $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to almost colourless $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ in acid.

questions.question: Butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate. What is the major organic product?
questions.answer: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone.

questions.question: The infrared spectrum of an organic compound is shown. The compound could be:
questions.answer: A broad O–H absorption near 3300 cm⁻¹ with C–H and no C=O peak indicates an alcohol.

questions.question: 1.27 g samples of these substances are treated with excess dilute HCl. Which releases the greatest mass of carbon dioxide?
questions.answer: Each gives 1 mol $\text{CO}_2$ per mole, so the lowest molar mass ($\text{BeCO}_3$, 69 g mol⁻¹) gives the most.

questions.question: $2\text{NO}(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-62$ kJ mol⁻¹. Two successive changes were imposed on an equilibrium mixture, with the effects shown. Which changes best account for the graph?
questions.answer: The gradual first shift to the left shows a temperature rise; the sudden drop in NO shows NO was removed.
options: First: temperature decreased. Second: partial pressure of O₂ increased.
First: temperature decreased. Second: partial pressure of NO decreased.
First: temperature increased. Second: partial pressure of O₂ increased.
First: temperature increased. Second: partial pressure of NO decreased.

questions.question: Which of the compounds shown is both an amine and a ketone?
questions.answer: B has a C=O between two carbons (ketone) and a separate $\text{NH}_2$ group. A is an aldehyde, C an amide, D has an ether oxygen.

questions.question: A conductometric titration of an acid with a base of similar concentration gave the graph shown. The acid and base could have been:
questions.answer: Conductivity falls to almost zero because $\text{BaSO}_4$ precipitates and water forms, removing nearly all ions.

questions.question: A colourless organic liquid is tested: (1) bromine water gives a yellow-brown solution; (2) acidified potassium dichromate stays yellow-orange; (3) sodium hydrogen carbonate gives a colourless solution and bubbles of colourless gas. Which functional group(s) may be present?
questions.answer: Gas with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ indicates a carboxylic acid; no decolourisation (no C=C) and no oxidation.
options: Hydroxyl group on a secondary carbon

questions.question: Which row correctly matches a reaction type with its reactants, catalyst and product?
questions.answer: Hydrogenation of ethene over nickel is an addition reaction giving ethane.

questions.question: $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)+\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_3(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Fe(C}_7\text{H}_5\text{O}_3)^{2+}(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)$. The yield of the violet complex may be decreased by:
questions.answer: Lowering the pH adds $\text{H}^+$, shifting equilibrium to the left.

questions.question: For 2-methylbutane (shown), which splitting pattern appears in the ¹H NMR spectrum for the circled $\text{CH}_3$ group?
questions.answer: Its neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$ has two H atoms, so by the $n+1$ rule it is a triplet.

questions.question: For ethyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which species produces the molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum?
questions.answer: The molecular ion is the molecule that has lost one electron.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the diagram of soap around oil?
questions.answer: Charged heads face the water while hydrocarbon tails dissolve in the oil.
options: The hydrophilic head is polar and attracted to water; the non-polar hydrophobic tails form micelles trapping oil.
The hydrophilic head is non-polar and attracted to water; the polar tails form micelles trapping oil.
The hydrophilic head is polar and attracted to oil; the non-polar tails form micelles trapping water.
The hydrophobic head is non-polar and attracted to water; the hydrophilic tails trap oil.

questions.question: Calculate the minimum concentration of a silver nitrate solution that will cause precipitation of silver bromide when 25.0 mL of it is added to 25.0 mL of 0.020 mol L⁻¹ sodium bromide. ($K_{sp}(\text{AgBr})=5.35\times10^{-13}$)
questions.answer:
$\text{AgBr}(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{Br}^-(aq)$.

After mixing, volumes double: $[\text{Br}^-]=0.010$ mol L⁻¹.

Precipitation begins when $Q=K_{sp}$: $[\text{Ag}^+]=\dfrac{5.35\times10^{-13}}{0.010}=5.35\times10^{-11}$ mol L⁻¹ in the mixture.

The original solution was diluted by half, so $c(\text{AgNO}_3)=$ **$1.07\times10^{-10}$ mol L⁻¹**.

questions.question: The seeds of cycad plants are used by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to make bread, but contain toxins including macrozamin and cycasin (shown). Explain the process used to remove these toxins, with reference to the structure of each molecule.
questions.answer:
The seeds are crushed or ground (increasing surface area) and then **leached**: placed in a woven bag and soaked in running water for days to weeks.

Both toxins are very water soluble because of their structures: macrozamin has **six** hydroxyl groups (two sugar rings) and cycasin has **four**, plus further polar O atoms. These form many hydrogen bonds with water.

Running water continually carries away the dissolved toxin, so the dissolution equilibrium (toxin(s) ⇌ toxin(aq)) is never established and keeps shifting right until almost all toxin is removed. The remaining insoluble starch can be made into bread.

questions.question:
Students standardised an approximately 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution with oxalic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4+2\text{NaOH}\to\text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, to analyse aspirin tablets.

Three 25.00 mL samples of 0.1034 mol L⁻¹ oxalic acid required an average of 25.75 mL of NaOH. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
What is the end point of a titration?
questions.answer: The point during a titration at which the indicator first shows a **permanent** colour change, signalling that the equivalence point has been reached.

questions.question:
Two aspirin ($\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$) tablets were dissolved in each of four flasks (water and ethanol) and titrated with 0.2008 mol L⁻¹ NaOH:
$\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4+\text{NaOH}\to\text{C}_9\text{H}_7\text{O}_4\text{Na}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$

| Trial | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume (mL) | 16.55 | 16.50 | 16.60 | 16.85 |

The packet claims 150.0 mg of aspirin per tablet. Calculate the mass of aspirin per tablet and justify whether the claim is true.
questions.answer:
Trial 4 is an outlier. Average of trials 1–3: 16.55 mL.
$n(\text{NaOH})=0.2008\times0.01655=3.323\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{aspirin})$
$m=3.323\times10^{-3}\times180.15=0.5987$ g in two tablets, so **299 mg per tablet**.

The claim is not true: the measured mass is about twice the stated 150 mg, a difference far larger than titration uncertainty.

questions.question: What is the maximum pH that can be obtained by dissolving $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ in pure water? ($K_{sp}=5.61\times10^{-12}$, 25 °C)
questions.answer:
$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Mg}^{2+}+2\text{OH}^-$. With solubility $s$: $K_{sp}=4s^3$, so $s=1.12\times10^{-4}$ mol L⁻¹.
$[\text{OH}^-]=2s=2.24\times10^{-4}$, pOH $=3.65$, **pH = 10.35** (saturated solution).

questions.question: The maximum pH of a saturated $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ solution is about 10.35. How does this compare with the maximum pH obtainable with NaOH? (The solubility of NaOH is 1.20 g mL⁻¹ at 25 °C.)
questions.answer:
$1.20$ g mL⁻¹ $=1200$ g L⁻¹, so $c=1200/40.0=30$ mol L⁻¹ $=[\text{OH}^-]$ (treating the volume as that of the solution).
pOH $=-\log30=-1.48$, pH $\approx15.5$.

This is about 5 pH units higher (over $10^5$ times the hydroxide concentration), because NaOH is very soluble and dissociates completely, whereas $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is only sparingly soluble. (The value is idealised: such concentrated solutions do not behave ideally.)

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide can form when nitrogen burns at high temperature: $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$.

Write the equilibrium expression for this reaction.

Nitrogen dioxide can form when nitrogen burns at high temperature: $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$.

Draw a graph of the forward and reverse reaction rates against time, from the moment $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ begin to react until after equilibrium is established at time A, continuing to time B.
questions.answer: The forward rate starts at its maximum and decreases as reactants are used. The reverse rate starts at zero and increases as $\text{NO}_2$ forms. The two curves meet by time A and then remain equal and constant (horizontal) to time B.

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide can form when nitrogen burns at high temperature: $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$.

On a graph of forward and reverse rates against time (equilibrium reached at time A), show and label the effect of carrying out the same reaction at a higher temperature.
questions.answer: At the higher temperature both rates are higher (the forward rate starts higher), equilibrium is reached **sooner** (before A), and the equal rates at equilibrium are greater than before.

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide can form when nitrogen burns at high temperature: $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$.

Draw curves showing how the concentrations of the three gases change with time, from the moment $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ (equal initial concentrations) begin to react until equilibrium at time E1, continuing to time E2.
questions.answer: $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ start at the same concentration and $\text{NO}_2$ at zero. $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ fall and $\text{NO}_2$ rises, with changes in the ratio 1 : 2 : 2 ($\text{O}_2$ falls twice as much as $\text{N}_2$; $\text{NO}_2$ rises by the same amount that $\text{O}_2$ falls). All curves level off at E1 and are horizontal from E1 to E2. (The graph shown also includes part (d), from E2.)

questions.question:
Nitrogen dioxide can form when nitrogen burns at high temperature: $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$. The system is at equilibrium. At time E2 the volume of the vessel is doubled, and equilibrium is re-established by time E3.

Show or describe how the concentrations of the three gases change from E2 to E3.
questions.answer: At E2 all three concentrations instantly **halve**. The system then shifts towards the side with more moles of gas (left, 3 mol compared with 2), partially restoring the pressure: $[\text{N}_2]$ rises slightly, $[\text{O}_2]$ rises by twice as much, and $[\text{NO}_2]$ falls (by the same amount as $\text{O}_2$ rises), until level at E3.

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, used in swimming pools, dissociates: $\text{HOCl}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^++\text{OCl}^-$. The graph shows the distribution of HOCl and OCl⁻ against pH at 25 °C.

What is the effect on pH when OCl⁻ ions are added to the water?
questions.answer: The pH **increases**: added $\text{OCl}^-$ combines with $\text{H}^+$ (the equilibrium shifts left), lowering $[\text{H}^+]$.

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, used in swimming pools, dissociates: $\text{HOCl}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^++\text{OCl}^-$. The graph shows the distribution of HOCl and OCl⁻ against pH at 25 °C.

At pH 8.5, what is the ratio $[\text{OCl}^-]:[\text{HOCl}]$?
questions.answer: From the graph, about 10% is HOCl and 90% is $\text{OCl}^-$, so the ratio is about **9 : 1**.

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, used in swimming pools, dissociates: $\text{HOCl}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^++\text{OCl}^-$. The graph shows the distribution of HOCl and OCl⁻ against pH at 25 °C.

Given that $[\text{OCl}^-]:[\text{HOCl}]=9:1$ at pH 8.5, calculate $K_a$ for hypochlorous acid.
questions.answer:
$[\text{H}^+]=10^{-8.5}=3.16\times10^{-9}$ mol L⁻¹.
$$K_a=\frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{OCl}^-]}{[\text{HOCl}]}=3.16\times10^{-9}\times9=2.8\times10^{-8}$$

*Note: the school's working sets $[\text{HOCl}]=\frac{10}{90}[\text{H}^+]$, which is not valid reasoning ($[\text{OCl}^-]\ne[\text{H}^+]$), although the final value is the same.*

questions.question: Two factories produce liquid wastes, one acidic and one basic. 25.0 mL of waste A required 29.5 mL of 0.233 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid for exact neutralisation. 25.0 mL of waste B required 32.8 mL of 0.274 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide. What volume of waste A should be mixed with 100.0 L of waste B to produce neutral waste?
Three unlabelled test tubes contain butan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol and hex-1-ene (all colourless). Describe chemical tests to identify each, including expected observations and relevant equations.
questions.answer:
**Test 1: bromine water.** Add a few drops to a sample of each and shake. Only **hex-1-ene** rapidly decolourises the orange-brown bromine water:
$\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH(CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3+\text{Br}_2\to\text{CH}_2\text{BrCHBr(CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3$
(in water, some bromo-alcohol also forms).

**Test 2: acidified potassium dichromate, warmed**, on fresh samples of the other two. **Butan-1-ol** (primary) is oxidised and the solution turns from orange to green:
$3\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}+2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}+16\text{H}^+\to3\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOH}+4\text{Cr}^{3+}+11\text{H}_2\text{O}$

**2-Methylpropan-2-ol** (tertiary) cannot be oxidised, so the solution stays orange.

questions.question: Kevlar is a strong polyamide prepared by the reaction shown. Draw (or give the structure of) a segment of Kevlar and explain the strength and uses of the polymer based on its structure.
questions.answer:
Condensation polymerisation (losing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) gives the segment:
$$-[\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{NH}]_n-$$
(para-substituted rings joined by amide links).

**Structure and strength:** the rigid benzene rings and amide links make long, nearly linear chains that pack closely side by side. Between neighbouring chains there are many **hydrogen bonds** (N–H to O=C), plus dipole–dipole forces, strong dispersion forces and stacking of the aromatic rings. A large amount of energy is needed to separate the chains, so Kevlar is very strong, stiff and heat resistant for its low density.

**Uses:** bullet-proof vests, protective gloves and clothing, ropes, tyres and sporting equipment.

questions.question:
A student carried out the synthetic pathway shown, starting from pent-1-ene.

Give the structural formulae of compounds B to F (B is the alcohol that leads to D).
questions.answer:
- **B**: pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- **C**: pentan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{OH}$
- **D**: pentan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- **E**: pentanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{COOH}$
- **F**: N-tert-butylpentanamide, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CONHC(CH}_3)_3$

(The flowchart allows B and C to be either isomer; because D and E are later distinguished as a ketone and an acid, B is the secondary and C the primary alcohol.)

questions.question: Draw the semi-structural formula of the section of the addition polymer of pent-1-ene that contains three monomer units.
questions.answer: $$-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(C}_3\text{H}_7)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(C}_3\text{H}_7)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(C}_3\text{H}_7)-$$

questions.question: In a synthesis from pent-1-ene, compound D is pentan-2-one and compound E is pentanoic acid. The spectra shown belong to one of them. Identify which, and justify using each spectrum.
Give the IUPAC name of the ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
questions.answer: Pentan-2-one.

questions.question: How many signals would you expect in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pentan-2-one? Why?
questions.answer: **Five** signals. The molecule has no symmetry, so each of its five carbon atoms (including the carbonyl carbon) is in a different chemical environment.

questions.question:
| Compound | Molar mass (g mol⁻¹) | Solubility in water |
|---|---|---|
| but-1-ene | 56 | insoluble |
| 1-fluoropropane | 62 | slightly soluble |
| propan-1-ol | 60 | soluble |
| ethanamide | 59 | soluble |

Explain the different water solubilities of these compounds, supporting your answer with at least one labelled diagram.
questions.answer:
Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds. A compound dissolves well if it can form interactions with water of comparable strength. The molar masses are similar, so dispersion forces are similar.

- **But-1-ene** is non-polar: only dispersion forces. It cannot replace water's hydrogen bonds, so it is insoluble.
- **1-Fluoropropane** has a polar C–F bond, giving dipole–dipole forces and only weak hydrogen-bond acceptance, with a non-polar chain: slightly soluble.
- **Propan-1-ol** has an O–H group that both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds: soluble.
- **Ethanamide** has C=O and $\text{NH}_2$ groups, allowing several hydrogen bonds with water: soluble.

Labelled diagram (propan-1-ol with water):
$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_7-\text{O}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}\cdots\cdots\text{O}^{\delta-}\text{H}_2$$
(dotted line = hydrogen bond between the alcohol H and a water O; water H atoms also bond to the alcohol O).

questions.question:
A spirit burner containing propan-1-ol was used to heat 112 g of water in an aluminium beaker, to determine the molar enthalpy of combustion.

0.543 g of propanol raised the water temperature from 19.0 °C to 37.5 °C. Calculate the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion. $M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH})=60.10$ g mol⁻¹.
questions.answer:
$q=mc\Delta T=112\times4.18\times18.5=8661$ J
$n=0.543/60.10=9.035\times10^{-3}$ mol
$\Delta H_c=-q/n=-9.59\times10^{5}$ J mol⁻¹ $=-959$ kJ mol⁻¹

questions.question:
A spirit burner containing propan-1-ol was used to heat 112 g of water in an aluminium beaker, to determine the molar enthalpy of combustion.

On replication, the experimental value was consistently much lower than the accepted value. Explain ONE change that would improve accuracy.
questions.answer: Much of the heat is lost to the surroundings instead of heating the water. Surrounding the burner and beaker with a draught shield (or moving the flame closer and adding a lid) reduces heat loss, so more of the energy released is measured and the value is closer to the accepted one.

questions.question: The molar heat of combustion of propan-1-ol is 2021 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the mass of propan-1-ol, in tonnes, required to produce 9605 MJ of energy.
questions.answer:
$n=\dfrac{9605\times10^3}{2021}=4753$ mol
$m=4753\times60.10=2.856\times10^5$ g $=$ **0.286 tonnes**

*Note: the school's working uses 9600 MJ instead of 9605 MJ, giving 0.285 t.*

questions.question: The molar heat of combustion of propan-1-ol is 2021 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy released per mole of carbon dioxide produced in the complete combustion of propan-1-ol.
questions.answer:
$2\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}(l)+9\text{O}_2(g)\to6\text{CO}_2(g)+8\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

Each mole of propanol gives 3 mol $\text{CO}_2$, so energy per mole of $\text{CO}_2=2021/3=$ **674 kJ**.
